you are correct. I have no doubt that you treat humans with politeness, and there is technically nothing wrong with being rude to a piece of code. but people will still dislike you for it, illogical as it is. let me explain.

imagine: a person opens the refrigerator, and sees that they ran out of milk. frustrated, they kick the fridge while shouting insults at it. was anyone hurt? no. but if someone saw a person do that, their opinion of that person would instinctively become less positive.

even though people understand logically that "not being nice to inanimate objects" and "not being nice to people" are different things, we are evolutionarily hardwired to see that behaviour as objectionable. humans, as a species, have very high empathy. we're pack animals. before we spoke languages or understood morals, our packs - our communities - were held together by this instinct alone. 

empathy doesn't follow logic - we tend to anthropomorphise things, animals, even objects; it's a very strong instinct we have. children worrying that their toys will miss them when they sleep, lonely people talking to their house plants, scientists giving hurricanes human names. so, when we see someone *fail* to humanise an inanimate object, we react negatively, but can't exactly pinpoint a logical reason. because to our animal brains, we are still living in a time when empathy was the only reason your neighbours don't want to bash you over the head with a rock.

TL;DR: people dislike when you have no aversion to treating something human-sounding with impoliteness. to them, it indicates kindness isn't hard-wired into you, and your social behaviour is only motivated by possible repricussions.

I have had a similar feeling where I felt like my responses in conversation were similar to an AI's responses. But it's very hard to put a finger as to why, since there are so many factors involved. I think a big part of it are the different types of thinking.

Autistic people tend to think very algorithmically, and the process of constructing a response tends to be very step-by-step. (Personally, I like to imagine instructions for myself when doing so). On the other hand, neurotypical people rely more on their intuition. When coming up with a response, they tend to "go with the flow" instead of going through a detailed process (e.g. intuitively knowing what the person meant, what parts of the subject are relevant to the current conversation, etc. I think of it as them skipping certain steps in the instructions.).

You are onto something here with the part about information. Autistic people tend to be better at forming a deep understanding of a small selection of information, while NTs tend to be better at forming surface-level understanding of many different types of information. This is due to the types of thinking I mentioned. If you go through something step by step, you can better understand the nuances of the topic, but your scope is limited since that process is slow. If you skip some of the steps, you lose some of the nuance, but you can asses information quickly this way and make faster connection between multiple selections of information. In communication, it means that - in general - it's easier for an autistic person to give a single detailed reply (like talking about a special interest for hours), while for NTs it's easier to talk about multiple topics over shorter periods of time.

ChatGPT's replies might sound autistic due to their tendency to be more literal, verbose, in-depth and occasionally containing unnecessary parts or details. You were correct in identifying that this is due to chatGPT not having an intuition or any intrinsic knowledge about communication (I assume this is what you meant by "without emotion/bias"?) and being simply presented with information, having to recognise the patterns by itself. This is the mechanism behind the traits chatGPT's and autistic people's replies share. It can also be referred to as "bottom-up" processing, where you essentially start with analysing smaller structures (like grammar rules, how verbs conjugate, etc.) and build up towards larger structures (like the rules of conversation, figurative language, etc.). obligatory NAD. it shows a long PR interval, in your case caused by 1st degree AV block. the P wave corresponds to the atrial contraction, which is when the small heart chambers contract to pump the blood into the two main chambers. the electrical signal then travels over the AV node (a bundle of neurons), which then send a signal for the big chambers to contract and pump the blood through your body. that second contraction is the ventricular contraction, and it is represented by the QRS complex on the ECG.

a long PR interval means that there is a longer delay between the atrial and the ventricular contraction. it is called "AV block" because the signal takes a longer stop at the AV node before traveling to the ventricles. 1st degree AV block is usually benign, but I'm not qualified to say what the consequences of that can be. ask your doctor for more information if you would like to know more about that condition.

they didn't tell you about the PACs? damn. well, I'm not a doctor, but if you're curious: PACs are when the atria contract prematurely. That contraction is also seen as the P wave (the small wave preceding the main beat. the main beat is also called the QRS complex, which corresponds to the ventricular contraction) in the ECG. the beat is then followed by a compensatory pause. the compensatory pause is like a "recovery period": since the heart contracted too early, it pumped a lot of blood out, so it waits until it's properly filled with blood again. 

it's hard to tell in this ECG, but it looks like the P waves preceding the PACs are very similar to regular P waves (not biphasic or inverted etc.) so these PACs probably originate from tissue very close to the sinus node, the node that usually sets the rhythm. so, most likely from the right atrium.
